# **TRANSFORMATIONAL WEBINARS SCRIPTS**

Establish authority, create commitment and handle objections right upfront  
We don’t really handle them we go at them, we go at them hard

Foster Hope for a better tomorrow  
Create intrigue so that people will want to stick around and watch the whole webinar, that’s what we do with the introduction

IN THE CONTENT    
We show a clearly defined outcome  
Here’s our agenda today and here’s what you’re going to accomplish by the end of the Webinar and we teach it, Step by Step  
FOR EACH STEP we provide context vision strategy and commitment

TRANSITION  
And CLOSE

All the elements do not necessarily need to be in the exact order you just need to have them there… 

The framework is divided into five sections: Introduction, Content, Transition, Close, and Time.


## **Introduction (5-15 minutes)**

What would success look like to you?

What are you willing to commit to realize that success?

What mindsets do you need to adopt for you to be successful?

How can you make success a certainty?

The introduction is designed to build rapport and establish your authority. It should include elements such as:  

* ### **Authority:** 

  Establishing authority is the most crucial aspect of a webinar introduction. It ensures your audience perceives you as credible, knowledgeable, and worth listening to.   
  Demonstrate your expertise through results, positioning, celebrity endorsements, or testimonials.  

  Implementation: Use a story-driven approach to seamlessly weave authority-building elements into your introduction. Avoid sounding boastful; instead, present these points as natural parts of your journey. People trust authority, and authority sells.  
  A webinar with weak authority will struggle to engage audiences, whereas strong authority will create immediate trust and excitement, making it much easier to sell later

  ***1\. Results*** – Share measurable success stories. Whether it's revenue figures, conversion rates, or industry achievements, concrete results validate your expertise.  
  What have you been able to accomplish personally that is remarkable and out of the ordinary? Your results, or other people’s results or your clients results…   
  Just as important as your own results is how you show them.In ﬁgure 1, 

  I showed the actual leaderboard, not a slide with numbers I typed out. 

  In ﬁgure 2, I showed a text message exchange with my business partner, who was updating me on sales numbers during  the actual webinar.You’ll hear me say this time again—show and tell. Not just tell.As much as possible, present your proof in the real world,even if it’s not that pretty.

  ###    **Positioning:** 

  Establish your *credibility by associating yourself with elite groups, prestigious events, or high-level investments. Example: "I paid $25,000 to join Genius Network."*

  *What about you could you show that would be impressive and set you apart from others they may compare you to?* *Who are you compared to other people that could talk on this topic about what makes you special… You want to set yourself apart from everybody else.* 

  Positioning is putting yourself and the information you share in relation to what you already know about the audience.

  Positioning Then-And-Now  
  You should also consider positioning yourself to be relatable to your audience. The best way of doing that is to show how you came from where they are now coming from.  
  3\. Celebrity: Do certain people in your field or in general think you’re a big deal? Can you prove it? You want to be head shoulders above. Celebrities means how do you make yourself look like a big deal? You as celebrities showing off all your cool stuff… Everything that could make people think oh wow that person is a big deal… Show them what it is like working with you. Showing them that working with you is way better than not working with you.

  CELEBRITY  
  This is the third element to cementing your authority status. There are three types of celebrities: (1) global, (2) local, and (3) manufactured.  
  Global is the one most often thought of when we talk about celebrities. These are the people pretty much everyone knows. As cheesy as it is, you should take every chance you can to get a shot with a celebrity.   
  What does that have to do webinars? Nothing. But people are impressed by celebrities, and they are also impressed if you have met celebrities.  
  Listen, I don’t care if that celebrity has nothing to do with your topic—people are impressed by people who meet celebrities.  
  Here, you’re getting authority by proxy. Plus, it’s easy to and a way to connect it. For the webinar on webinars, I can explain that my marketing power is so strong I get to be in private rooms with people like Shaquille O’Neal.

  Important—don’t overdo celebrity. Treat it like salt. A little bit goes a long way, but too much of it can ruin everything.  
  If you don’t have a celebrity, it doesn’t mean the world is over. I sold well for years without any celebrity. It’s just harder. If you don’t have it right now, make it a priority to get some as soon as possible, because it will only help.  
  4\. Testimonials: If you promise to help those on the webinar, who have you helped with this same thing before the webinar? 

  TESTIMONIALS  
  This is probably the weakest area of most people’s webinars.  
  Which is a travesty, because testimonials are one of the most powerful resources you can use to make a sale.  
  Yet how do most webinar presenters use testimonials?  
  Almost as an afterthought. They cram it into the pitch in a big, long chunk—rolling out one testimonial after another perfunctorily.  
  That’s not how you do it. If testimonials are so powerful, you should use them all throughout your presentation, and especially in your introduction.  
  I have a rule: ve testimonials in the first five minutes. You shouldn’t spend much time on these, but they should show up.

  Types of Testimonials  
  These are the types of testimonials you can use in your  
  introduction:  
  1\. Character testimonial: Someone who talks about how good you are as a person and at what you do. Ideally, this person is a celebrity or someone of clout and influence.  
  2\. Big results testimonial: Someone with an exceptional, specific, tangible outcome. Like John Carter doing seven figures.  
  3\. Initial results testimonial: Someone who, as a result of seeing a webinar like the one you’re doing, got some sort of immediate result, even if it’s a modest one.  
  4\. Inspirational testimonial: Someone whose life was so dramatically impacted as a result of learning from you, that it transcended just the benets related to the topic at hand.  
  Most presenters barely get any of these four elements in their introductions. As such, they have little to no authority established.  
  You should be able to, within the first few minutes of your webinar, establish authority at a level almost unmatchable by anyone else in your industry who is using webinars.


* ### **Commitment:** 

  Get the audience to "buy in" to your presentation, which will lead to them buying your product or service.    
  Get an early commitment. Hey I’m going to show you this and if I do this will you PROMISE To put it in action if it makes sense to you?   
  Some type of commitment should be there before I sell anything on a webinar to anyone. I first want them to have some kind of commitment there to put that in action. If they see themselves to put that in action in their mind then it would be much much easier to buy a solution that helps them achieve that when it comes time to make the offer. 

  What is certainly true though is most webinar attendees don’t hear or listen. If they do, it’s done passively. You want active listening. The more favorable pictures and movies you can get them to create in their minds in relation to your presentation, the more you’ll sell. Plain and simple.  
  It’s one thing to say, “My goal here today is to show you how to create webinars that make you more money in your life than you could ever hope to spend...” in my webinar introduction. It’s quite another if I add this: “...and if I make you a bunch more money, can I get you to promise you’ll spend just a little of that with me and my company in the future?”  
  Much better. Yet, why stop there when we can also ask, “Let me know if that’s okay with you by typing yes into the chat box.”  
  What have we done here? We have put the idea and image in their mind of spending money with us. Not only that, we got them to write it down. It’s amazing how much this little act of writing can make a big difference.  
  In the first ve minutes, you have to get them, in writing, to tell you that they will commit to something major. Not only does this foreshadow a relationship where you tell them to do something and they do it, but also hopefully the thing you ask is in alignment with your offer at the end.  
  *“My agenda today is, in our small amount of time together, to give you little effort strategies that provide big impact in your business and life. My aim is to create confidence where there once was uncertainty. To shatter confusion and replace it with clarity. To give, share, and show exactly what to do, when to do it, and how to do it. My goal is to unlock within you the true potential I know you have inside so that you can make your unique and wonderful dent in the universe. Oh, if we can’t do all of that, at least there is one thing I know I can do for you today—and that’s to make you money. Lots of it. Yet, this is a two-way street. I am going to give you my A-level best for our brief time we are together today, because I have faith that you will actually use what I share with you. Nothing pains me more, nothing hurts me deeper, tha someone encountering a life-changing idea and letting it go to waste. So I’m going to give you my best, but in return I ask you for your best. I ask you right now, as we go through this, to see yourself doing what I show you. To make it yours, to see the future show up right now in the present, because as a friend and mentor, Bob Proctor told me ‘Thoughts become things. If you see it in your mind, you will hold it in your hand.’ And I want you to think about what I show you today. And if you do that, you will hold it in your hand. Lots and lots and lots of it. Is it okay for us to move forward  with this agreement in place? Don’t just nod your head or say it to yourself. This is serious study. Prove it to me with the simplest, yet most powerful of gestures—a ‘yes’ in the chat box right now.”*  
  Heck, I didn’t even get them to just think about using it. I got them to promise me to give me their best. In writing.  
  Commitments create identities. The stronger the identity,the more congruence there will be with actions in line with that identity. If you’re someone who agrees with me that you’re going to give it your best, and then I set up a situation where not investing with me is not giving me your best, that incongruence is going to cause you pain. The compliance, on the other hand, will bring you pleasure.  
    
  To look at it from another perspective, if you don’t get a commitment, you run the risk of never getting them on the same page as you—and to me, that’s being careless with their time and yours.  
  In the introduction, you get that mega-commitment—that thing, in one sentence, that gets them to make a promise to you that, during the webinar, they will do something which (a) creates pictures and movies in their mind that make them more favorable to your offer, and (b) lets them see themselves taking action on what you’re showing them. If you don’t want to be creative, just take my previous example  
  above and modify it. Then run with it.  
  Commitment orientates your audience toward the future, not the past. Most people who can’t make progress around a challenge often look to the past when thinking about solutions.  
  That doesn’t work. Yet it seems to be hardwired in almost all of us. If you study the greatest geniuses, the truly creative problem solvers, they had the ability to look into the future and practically bring it to the present. Commitment up front allows you to give them that big, juicy future as a target in their mind in the present. That’s why commitment is so important.

  *“Jason Fladlien here, and if you’re hearing my Iowa-accented voice and you see on your screen right now a slide that says‘ webinar will be starting soon,’ arm for me in the chat box.And while you’re at it, let’s spice it up. Give me a ‘yes’ without using the word ‘yes’...Angela says ‘oh yeah.’ Marcus says ‘ten-four.’ Justin says ‘loud and clear.’ Lia says ‘affirmative.’ Antonio says ‘copy that.’ Tina says ‘absolutely,’ and I’m getting ‘alright,’ and ‘certainly,’ and ‘thumbs up,’ and ‘sure thing,’ and even an ‘amen’ thrown in there for good measure. Excellent\! We’re off to a good start then...”*  
  What did I accomplish here? I showed my audience there are a lot of different ways to say yes to something and that it’s fun to say yes to something.

  I first conceptualized this technique because of a study I once read where they had people watching a bouncing ball go up and down, to simulate head nodding, and then afterwards tested to see if that influenced them to be more likely to say yes to moderately large requests. Turns out, it does. (By the way, it works the other way also. I saw a Blimpies commercial once where they were shaving ham in a back and forth, left to right motion, and as your head follows it, you are shaking your head no. I bet that ad didn’t perform well.)  
  When I do my webinar on how to start an Amazon business,  
  I get my audience in the introduction to say out loud, “I sell  
  my own line of products on Amazon.” Then I have them  
  type into the chat how that made them feel, and I play off  
  those powerful emotions throughout the rest of the webinar.


* ### **Objections:** 

  Address any potential objections the audience may have.   
  Listen. Objections are so devastating toward sales that we don’t “handle” them. You handle ne china. We take objections and we devastate their entire existence. I don’t just dislike objections, they disgust me.  
  Many people are only one tiny, little excuse away from making major progress in certain areas of their life. Most people let little concerns cheat them out of great big leaps of progress.  
  Bring the objections upfront…   
  Sit down and think about what are the 4-5 objections that your audience are likely to use as an excuse to stay small? 

  Many people are only one tiny, little excuse away from making major progress in certain areas of their life. Most people let little concerns cheat them out of great big leaps of progress.  
  Because objections are so insidious we can’t wait until later on to smash them. We must start in the introduction. Now,this is markedly different than how most webinar presenters treat objections. They usually do so only casually in the content section, if that. The focus on “handling” objections, in their mind, is reserved for the close. Not good enough.  
    
  We apply different pressure on the objections in the introduction, sure. Think of it as first weakening the foundation of the objection before we bring in the demolition crew.  
  How do we handle those? How to completely destroy them…  In the introduction we don’t completely go into too much detail about the objections but we at least address them otherwise people will bring them to their mind throughout the webinar and use it later as an excuse to justify their inaction.   
  You can say something on the line,YES it’ll still work for you even if you are on a limited budget… YES it’ll still work for you even if you have a  full time job right now and don’t have much time… YES it’ll still work for you even if you did not have any previous experience… No it’s not an issue for you if you …blank…  
  Bring these up YES it’ll still work for you even if dot dot dot…

Also note the combinations of techniques. I handle objections while showing testimonials. I get commitment on the last testimonial—that’s two major commitments I’ve drawn upon in the introduction.

	**OBJECTION SMASHING**

How do you go about constructing your own objection smashing in the introduction?

First, you start with the key objections. Every offer has a combination of universal objections and topic-specific objections. An example of a universal objection are  money and time.  
I always assume time and money will be major objections  
going in. In addition, here are some other universal objections that  
tend to consistently show up across most markets you’d nd  
yourself doing webinars in.

**• Belief:** You’ve tried to solve this problem before and you couldn’t. You’ve failed every time previous to this. Why should this time be different?

**• Ability:** Could you even learn this given all the time and resources in the world? Some skills are harder to pick up than others, or are biasedly easier/harder for  
some people.

**• Trust:** Does it sound too good to be true? Why should they have any faith that you’re here to help them beyond just getting them to spend money?  
**• Fear:** Usually the fear of change, the fear of failure, the fear of the unknown, or a combination of all of those things.  
**• Conflict:** They want to get out of a situation they’re  
currently in, but don’t see how they can do so without betraying the essence of who they are. How can you give them an out and/or show this isn’t a valid concern?  
**• Confusion**: Where do they start, how do they nish, can they do it if \[*insert supposed unique situation here\]*?  
**• Timing**: Is now the right time for them? Did they miss the boat? Is it too early for them?

Even though these are universal objections, it doesn’t mean  
that you will use them for each and every webinar, though  
you probably will end up doing so in the content and pitch  
section more often than not.

In the introduction, you’ll probably use time, money, and  
one or two of these additional universal benets.  
Next, there are product-specific objections. Examples: 

Things I believe my audience is worried about that might prevent their success with webinars:

• How do I get people to attend my webinars?  
• What system and technology should I use?  
• Do I have to hard sell like Jason does?  
• Will it apply specifically to the goods and services I offer?

Will it apply specifically to the goods and services I offer?

Here’s how I handle this:

*“Now, these techniques I’m going to show you today have a*  
*caveat. They don’t work in every market. They only work in*  
*markets that meet the following criteria—the person you’re*  
*selling to is a human being. This doesn’t work on dogs and*  
*cats and aliens from other dimensions. Yet, all humans have*  
*basic primal decision making hardwired in them from the last 200,000 years of existence. So if you’re selling something worthwhile that helps someone, there is a high degree of certainty that this will work for you. Put that aside for now,*  
*though, and let this wash over you, and then at the end you’ll*  
*know more if this will be the perfect thing for you to use with*  
*your own customers and your products. Now, having done*  
*this before a few thousand times, I can tell you the odds are*  
*largely in your favor.”*

Every objection can be dealt with one of three ways: (1) ignorance, (2) disagreement, or (3) agreement.

Ignorance is choosing to ignore the objection or pretending it doesn’t exist. You never want to ignore major objections. You may decide not to take them on or bring them up in  
the introduction, but you should never ignore them. Small objections? Sure, you can choose to ignore them in the introduction or ignore them altogether.

Disagreeing with an objection is the most common way of  
challenging it. However, it’s rarely advised you do it like this:  
“If you think you can’t do this, you’re a moron. You stupid  
idiot, of course you can do it, and I’m going to show you how.”

Instead, here is the common formula you can default to:

*“You may be wondering whether you can or can’t do what*  
*I’m going to share with you today. That is a valid concern,*  
*because what you’re really wanting to know is this—will this*  
*time be different? Will you finally get the solution you’ve*  
*been looking for all this time? I believe you can, and as we*  
*go through the presentation today, I’m going to show you*  
*how this unique approach seems to work for all different people from all different backgrounds—each and every one*  
*with their own unique set of challenges they bring to the*  
*table. So look for that, and it should help you see that you,*  
*in fact, can do this.”*

***Here is the formula behind it: (1) acknowledge and soften,***  
***(2) validate and reframe, and (3) present a target.***

Acknowledge and soften.

“You may be wondering whether you can or can’t do what I’m going to share with you today.”

Wondering is a soft word. Worry is a hard word. So we use wondering.  
“You may be” is a soft phrase. “You absolutely are” is a hard phrase. So we use “you may be.” We acknowledge the objection, while simultaneously diminishing the bite  
of the objection.

**Validate and reframe.**  
Validation gets you rapport because it’s like you’re reading  
their mind. Reframing allows you to point the objection to something favorable instead of something unfavorable.  
In the example above, here’s how I did it: “That is a valid concern because what you’re really wanting to know is will this time be different? Will you finally get the solution you’ve been looking for all this time?” Not too creative on the validation front. I just plain used the phrase “that’s a valid concern.” The reframe is masterful, though.

Notice how I moved the focus from “can you do this?” to “will you be able to do this?” Naturally, they wouldn’t be on the webinar if there weren’t some part of them that wishes and wants to believe that this time will be different. I just  
switched their focus from failure to possibility. That's a reframe. I could’ve just as easily done it like this: “I get it, because I was you and that’s what was on my mind. At the heart of it, though, what I discovered was I really wasn’t so troubled by could I do or couldn’t I...what changed it for me was when I said ‘What would it take for me to...’”

Same thing—validate and reframe. Different words, same pattern.

Present a target.  
“I believe you can, and as we go through the presentation today, I’m going to show you how this unique approach seems to work for different people from all different backgrounds, each and every one with their own unique set of challenges they bring to the table. So look for that, and it should help you see that you, in fact, can do this.”  
If you give people clear targets, they are more likely to comply.  
If you tell them to look for something, they will likely find it.  
Here, what we tell them to look for is evidence that validates  
that they can do it. What do you think happens when you  
give them that target?  
You master this disagreement technique for objections and  
your ability to sell in any situation will improve.

	The last way to deal with an objection is to agree with it.

Agreeing with an objection is the ultimate form of validation. Remember this example: 

“Now these techniques I’m going to show you today have a caveat: they don’t work in every market.” 

 Boom\! By saying this, I get a deeper rapport with an audience than I ever could get if I disagreed, even though this is what I follow it up with:

“This only works in markets that meet the following criteria: the person you’re selling to is a human being. This doesn’t work on dogs and cats and aliens from other dimensions.” 

I agreed and at the same time changed what we were agreeing on. I did so by bypassing the resistance that can occur when you disagree with someone. Thus, the agreement frameworks like this: (1) agree with their objection, (2) define what you’re agreeing to, (3) prove it to be true, and (4) provide a target.

We agreed it doesn’t work in some markets. We defined that it only works in markets with human beings. Here is how we prove it: “All humans have basic primal decision  
making them hardwired in them from the last 200,000 years of existence, so if you’re selling something worthwhile that helps someone, there is a high degree of certainty that this will work for you.”

Lastly, provide the target. “Put that aside for now, though, and let this wash over you, and then at the end you’ll know more if this will be the perfect thing for you to use with our customers and your products. Now, having done this before a few thousand times, I can tell you the odds are largely in your favor.”  
Note: targets become more direct as you get to the close. In the pitch, the target is usually, “Because you and I know this to be true, what you need to do next is obvious—go to that URL you see on your screen, and let’s get started by  
signing up now.”  
Finally, there is an advanced technique in relation to dealing

with objections in the introduction: include by excluding. President Donald Trump is an example of this. By repelling more people than he attracted, he became the leader of the free world. You can agree with an objection in the introduction  
where you absolutely will turn off a portion of your audience from buying. Just try to pick that portion who wouldn’t buy anyway and who, by turning off, you turn on even more the people who are likely to buy.

	Here’s an example with the objection of “Will webinars work in my business?”

*“What I’m going to show you today does indeed have limitations and is not applicable to each and every market. Webinars won’t do your dishes for you and clean your house. They have a specific application, and if at any point in the content you feel like they don’t apply to you, then you’re probably right. However, the ip is also true. If you see, as we go through this, that this does apply to you, then congratulations\! I’m going to make you so much money that you’ll probably end up wanting to name one of your kids after me...”*

#### 	***HUMOR IN SELLING***

You may notice I sometimes use humor. I rarely use humor outside of the introduction. I do so to put the attendee at ease.

Since we’re just weakening the foundation of the objections in the introduction, I’m using a bit more finesse. If I can get them to laugh at their “problem” now, it’s easier to destroy that problem later as it relates to making the sale.

The majority of people you’re attempting to influence on a  
webinar are not optimistic about their chances, in spite of  
what they will tell you and what they tell themselves.  
Lasting change is truly, remarkably hard to obtain. Most  
things they have invested in to bring change in their life—  
even things that are not at all related to the problem or  
solution they are seeking—have usually produced no real  
results. Just more pain.

They bring all that with them into the webinar. If you let them focus just on that pain, it’s hard for them to see the world or your solution in any other light. This is why we must foster hope of a brighter, better future.

* ### **Intrigue:** 

  **(intriguing intro \+ hook):** Pique the audience's curiosity and make them want to learn more.    
  One of the reasons you want to set up mystery and intrigue  
  in the introduction is because how you reveal your insights  
  is even more important than the insights you reveal.  
  Also, it captivates. People don’t attend your webinars in prison cells. They have the choice of staying on the webinar or leaving. They have the choice of listening intently or treating the webinar as background noise.  
  By creating that mystery and intrigue in the opener, you’ve  
  dramatically increased their chances of actively listening  
  and participating for the rest of the webinar.  
  **FIRST, LAST TECHNIQUE**  
  The burned-down-house story is an advanced way of creating mystery and intrigue. A simpler, more methodical way of accomplishing this is what I call the “first, last” technique.  
  When creating my webinar, if nothing else, in the introduction I’ll put a slide that says, “On this webinar...\[ll this out later\].” Then, after the full webinar is finished, or at least the first shippable version, I’ll go back to that slide and start writing “blind bullets” to tease the things I will reveal later on the webinar. A blind bullet is where you promise them a benet, but you keep how to get that benet a secret.  
  If you were to read just the bullets, here is how they’d read:  
  • A detailed breakdown of the webinar framework I used to generate over $100 million in sales over the last eight years  
  • How to create more buyers in the introduction than most people do during their webinar pitch  
  • A webinar “magic trick” that helped us generate over  
  $1,400,000 in less than seventy-ve minutes  
  • A “content” formula so powerful you will nd it useful  
  in all areas of your business (not just for webinars)  
    
  • You’re most likely committing this mistake and it’s rob-  
  bing you blind  
    
  • A pitch formula that is so ll-in-the-blanks yet sooooooo profitable  
  I wrote those bullets points after I created the rest of the  
  presentation. Then I turned them into slides. Since I had the  
  luxury of doing this after the presentation was done, I could  
  also SHOW, not just tell. I showed parts of the slides to come.  
  I even foreshadowed the offer, as you can see in figure 18\.  
  Not only did I create mystery and intrigue to hook the audience in, but it allowed me to make my points land with more  
    
  impact when I revealed them.  
  When I show the ll-in-the-blanks pitch formula at the end, it  
  won’t be the first time they’ve seen it. Recognition enhances  
  the perception of value. If they’ve seen it before, and they  
  see it again, for whatever reason it seems to become more  
  valuable as long as it’s not redundant, repetitive, and boring.  
  Start with this “first, last” technique because it requires  
  minimal thought on your part. Tease what they’ll discover  
  on the webinar, but script this out after you’ve created the  
  actual content section of your webinar. When most people  
  throw around jargon like open loops, they think it means  
  one open loop. If you want to get technical, what I’m doing  
  is here is creating nested loops—open loops upon open loops,  
  and even loops within loops. I also do not close these loops  
  in chronological order. There is no obvious order, which is  
  done intentionally because the randomness increases the  
  attentiveness of the attendees.

## **Content (45-60 minutes)**

The content section is where you deliver the value proposition of your webinar.

Here is the one thing you are going to be able to do by the end of this webinar  
It should be very specific  
It should be concrete and it should be a thing that people think is unlikely to happen.

Real learning only occurs if it leads to behavior change, it will revolutionize how you deliver content on your webinars.

What causes true behavioral change? Emotion. It’s not just what you know, it’s how you feel about what you know.

When constructing the content section of your webinar, it’s  
okay the fIrst time to spew out way too much content in terms  
of the length of time it will take you to deliver it—because  
you’ll polish it down. As you polish, you also repeatedly do  
ecological checks.

So you do each step by revealing what the STEP is and then giving them CONTEXT, VISION and asking them if they are committed to put the Step in practice.   
This is just a really simple framework that helps people easily grasp new information with the mindset of not just to learn but to be TRANSFORMED. 

Using education, not just education but transformational education  
Education for the purpose of transformation  
Showing them education in a way that they are less scared but more empowered  
If you educate them in a way that they feel empowered than scared related to your solution.

**ECOLOGICAL CHECKS**

An ecological check is a Neuro-linguistic Programming (NLP)  
concept that helps you check your own feelings as they relate  
to deciding a course of action to take. I’ve used this same  
technique, but put myself in the shoes of my attendees.  
When doing ecological checks on your webinar content, here  
are some of the things you look for:  
• What emotional state does this put them in?  
• What are the downsides of acting or thinking about acting on this?  
• How does this make them feel about the future?  
• Why is this better than doing nothing at all or doing something completely different?  
• How important is this anyway? Does it truly matter?  
• How does this relate to the beliefs and values they likely hold true?  
• What is the price they’ll pay in effort to realize this, and is it worth it?

The first time I go through the content section, I’m not consciously thinking about any of that stuff. I’m just putting as much “how to” as I think is appropriate. On the second pass through of the content section, I whittle it down by getting rid of the superfluous, while molding the content to fit in with the emotional states I feel are most likely to make a sale later in the webinar.  
Finally, I punch up the remaining content to heighten the  
emotional states that will help empower my audience into  
action, while bringing them closer to buying what I’m selling  
at the end of the webinar.  
The following are universal emotions that I most often rely  
on in my webinars and that you’re likely to encounter as you  
create your content.

**FEAR**

This emotion costs more sales than any other. No matter how much someone wants something, if they’re scared of the potential consequences, they’ll more than likely do nothing at all instead of trying to improve their current position.

A big fear is being embarrassed. What will others think of  
them? Most people’s identities are wrapped up in how others  
perceive them to be, so they’d rather not jeopardize this  
identity if they don’t have to. Is any portion of your content  
creating fear, and if so—should you get rid of it? Or if you  
keep it—can you minimize or remove that fear?  
Equally or arguably more important is the flip side. Can you  
associate that fear with inaction—the listener not doing what  
you’re saying? Can you show them how the future will continue  
to get worse if they don’t do what you’re telling them to do?  
Make the fear of inaction stronger than the fear of trying  
something new and unknown.

**CONFUSION**

There’s a saying that a confused mind says no. That’s not accurate. A confused mind usually doesn’t say anything because it’s too confused to say yes or no.  
Later, I’ll show you how we use a technique called “roadmapping” to present content in a way that automatically diminishes the ability for the prospect to become confused.  
In addition, as you edit down your content section, make sure what you are showing them will create confidence and not confusion related to your topic.  
Your goal is to present your content in a way that removes confusion and uncertainty.

**ENTHUSIASM**

Ever been struck with an idea so compelling you dropped whatever you were doing to immediately pursue it?

That’s the kind of enthusiasm you want to foster in your content. How can you share your content so it’s harder for the attendee to sit still than to act on the content?

Your voice is one of the best ways to create enthusiasm. On my webinars, you can hear the excitement in my voice. It becomes contagious\! If you’re excited to teach it, they’ll be more excited to learn it.

**SAFETY**

Can you teach in a way that eliminates downsides and  
maximizes upsides? Show them that not doing what you’re  
teaching is the least safe option. Expand safety outside of  
the attendee and relate it to the world around them.  
Trust is one of the easiest ways to create safety—which is  
why we spent so much time on establishing your authority  
at the beginning. Make sure you maintain that authority  
throughout the content section as well, because otherwise  
you can jeopardize that feeling of safety.

**ANGER**

If you can get people upset at something and then show how your content is either a way to release that anger or that your technique destroys something morally outrageous—a great injustice—more people will act on that than just about anything.

Mob mentality is a powerful motivator.

One word of caution: anger can easily turn against the person who is inciting it. If you choose to use this emotion directly, be careful.

With that said, my favorite way of using anger is to get them upset with me about something. I’ll say something like, “Doesn’t it make you mad that someone like me with little college education, no formal business training, and a high, nasal-voice can do this and you can’t? What do you think the difference is...?”

By getting them red up to prove me wrong, it increases their desire to buy my product. I hope they do prove me wrong\!

**LONELINESS**

Henry David Thoreau is often quoted as saying, “The mass of  
men lead lives of quiet desperation.” They rarely quote the rest of it: “A stereotyped, but unconscious despair is concealed even under what are called the games and amusements of mankind.”  
Keyword: concealed. This concealment makes it hard to relate and connect to the world around them, and as such, they experience one of the most cutting emotions of all:  
loneliness. That is their desperation. As Janis Joplin put it, “On stage, I make love to 25,000 different people, then I go home alone.”  
When creating your content, you have to make sure that it doesn’t create a feeling of isolation or risk increasing loneliness or disconnection. On the other hand, if you can show them how what you teach them is the remedy for this disconnection and discontent, you can sell practically anything to that audience.

Your webinar Content must cause Identity SHIFT

If you shift Identity, You Shift Behavior… You want the outcome

Identity shifts behavior, Behavior shifts the outcome

98% of things you hear you will forget within 2 minutes in a conscious level.

You’re in the empowerment business

I empower people to get better outcome by shifting behavior

VISION – STRATEGY – TACTICS

Strategy is above tactics, above strategy is VISION.

IMPOVERISHED IDENTITY

Almost all people on your webinar have what I refer to as an impoverished identity.

If things were going good for them it’s unlikely, they’d even be on the webinar in the first place.

We must go to war against that impoverished identity to destroy it and put a stronger identity in its place in relation to the subject.

THEY COME IN COMPLETELY TRAUMATIZE

If you empower someone to do something they couldn’t do before you win the game.

Exaggerate to prove a point, one of the best ways to help someone get over their own issue is to make them angry related to their problems. Because now they feel like they some power over their problem, if they angry at their problem.

We can’t solve an identity issue with a tactical solution.

Show them first where they were capable… before addressing the issue.

Accelerate what they are already comfortable doing. It’s not about the technical or the tactical it’s about the mindset shift.

People are failing because they have an impoverished model of a reality.

Beat your competition in 20 minutes in your webinar. Start where they’re at.

How?

Remove a mental bloc. Shifting identity… If they’re scared the likelihood for them from acting is almost non-existent.

Make them compelled to act.

The content section is where you deliver the value proposition of your webinar. It should include elements such as:  

* ### **Defined Outcome:** 

  Clearly state what the audience will be able to do after watching your webinar.  

  All clearly defined outcomes must have an answer to this question: “How do I accomplish this in forty-ve to sixty minutes?” If you don’t think it’s possible, you have the wrong outcome defined. Most often, though, you’ll discover that it is possible with the right approach and care. When creating a clearly defined outcome, I first start with the audience.  
  The more narrowly you define your audience, the easier it is to achieve your outcome. Why? You can more specifically speak to their situation.  
  Once you identify your audience, the next step is determining what feeling you want them to experience. For example “easy, enjoyable” which create feelings of INSTANT GRATIFICATION  or “unmatchable advantage” which create feelings of SUPERIORITY.   
  The last part of the outcome is the result. When in doubt, build a result around instant gratification.  
  The question I ask myself is, “What’s something I can show  
  them that they could immediately do and see a result from  
  in the very near future?”

  The formula for a clearly defined outcome, then, is this:  
  1\. Audience: What audience are you going to serve?  
  2\. Feeling: What are they going to feel as they implement  
  what you teach?  
  3\. Result: What outcome would your audience consider  
  a success?  
    
  




* ### **Step by Step:** 

  Provide a clear and actionable plan that the audience can follow.    
  ![][image1]  
  Here’s the 5 things you need to do if you want this to happen…   
  And you list them all   
  The first thing is Step 1  
  The second thing is Step 2  
  The third thing is Step 3  
  The fourth thing is Step 4  
  The fifth thing is Step 5

  When it comes to creating a step-by-step process, follow this rule: no less than three steps, no more than five. If you have too few steps, it means you’ve probably combined two or more steps together.  
  If you have too many steps, either your defined outcome is overly-ambitious or your steps are too granular.  
  The best part about coming up with a step-by-step process is that you can show your audience.  
  Giving your audience a roadmap goes a long way toward getting rid of confusion as it relates to the content. It also creates an open loop—they don’t want to miss the next steps coming up\!  
  After we knock off a step, we note it on our “map.”  
  ![][image2]  
  Yours will likely look something like this, too. You usually start with more words than necessary. Over time, you’ll develop rhythm and cadence, and keep polishing your webinar to make it even more streamlined.  
  Once you have your step-by-step determined you’ll expand on those steps using a technique I created called “context, vision, commitment, strategy.”


* ### **Context:** 

  We don’t dive into the content saying STEP 1 do this… That’s the HOW of it but we want to wait on the HOW and give some context first… Most people need to know the Context before they need to know the Strategy  
  Say things like:  
  Here’s what you need to know about STEP 1 before we go into it  
  Here’s something interesting about STEP 1  
  Here’s WHY this matter  
  Things like that…  
  Before you give the Strategy and piece of advice give the CONTEXT first. 

  Inference is often the death of the sale. You don’t want your audience to infer. You want your audience calibrated before you jump into how to do each and every step. The first thing you need is context.  
  Before you show someone how to do something, you have to set the stage for why it’s important and what’s involved. I like to think of it as laying the ground rules to put the proper technique into the proper perspective.  
    
  The first part of context is often to answer the question:   
    
  “Why is this step crucial to your success?”  
    
  The second part of context is defining what is involved. For example for selecting products to sell on Amazon, over the next series of slides I explain:

  • Why we private label and what private labeling is  
  • What type of profit margins you can expect  
  • Why there are far more products available to sell than there are sellers to sell them 

  Ideally, within the context, you also increase desire to   
  implement.  
    
  Notice how the first bullet point in figure 24 says, “The more demand, the easier it is to sell in spite of yourself.”  
    
  I verbally expand on that bullet point by saying, “The better you are at picking products, the worse you can be at everything else.”  
  I’m getting them to desire wanting to pick better products   
  because they understand the importance. Guess what? In the offer itself, I have all sorts of cool bonuses that automate and help tremendously with product selection. I give them the manual approach during the content section, then offer the automatic approach and a whole bunch of other advantages during the pitch.  
    
  When I introduce the second bullet point in figure 24: “The Less competition, the quicker you can make profits,” I also say:

With what we’ve discovered, we Explain why the information you are sharing is important.*   With what we’ve discovered, we can and do beat any and everyone. However, certain products—just by the nature of showing up—can immediately bring in more money than should be possible.”  
    
  He goes on to explain that until you see the promise, you won’t endure the pain. I think of that story a lot when I think about context. Before showing them something new or different than what they are now doing (meaning, outside of their comfort zone), you have to get them to buy into a specific way that trumps any other way they could do it.  
    
  Buy-in leads to buying. The more they buy in with excitement about doing what you’re showing them at each step, the more likely they will buy at the end of the webinar.

* ### **Vision:** 

  Get the audience to visualize themselves taking action and achieving success.  Here’s what happens once you apply this.  
  Before giving the strategy you also want to give them the VISION first

  VISION  
  I think Wayne Dyer put it best when he flipped the saying “I’ll believe it when I see it\!” to “I’ll see it when I believe it.”
