* ### **Strategy:** 

  Provide more detailed steps or criteria to consider.    
  Strategy says HOW YOU APPLY THIS

  There are two ways I rely on teaching the “how” of the content portion of a webinar: steps or criteria.  
  Let’s look at step one in the Amazon webinar, product selection example.   
  Here is how I teach attendees to pick products on the webinar:  
  1\. Pick products that have proven buyer demand.  
  2\. Demand starts with best-seller rank in each and every   
  top-level category on Amazon.  
  3\. Filter that demand to an income stream you’d like to   
  show up in your life.  
  4\. Use tools to help assist you.  
  You could spend hours going into the ins and outs of just those four steps that, when combined, accomplish step one.   
  On strategy, I like to spend 30 percent to 35 percent of my time in the content section on step one alone.   
  Two reasons for this:   
  First, if you lose them on step one, you probably lose them for good. Second, pacing. We start “slow” and pick up the pace, and the tempo hits a frenzy right as we start our pitch.  
  Your goal is to, in about twenty minutes, show them the first step in a way they can easily wrap their heads around, feel confident being able to go out do it and see themselves (in their minds) actually doing and benefiting from using the first step.  
    
  *“Start in one of these categories, because we have a millionaire in each of these. Other categories are good I’m sure, but these I know for a fact can produce millionaires from scratch.”*  
  I do not read off the categories and, in fact, advance the slide quicker than they can probably write down or note the categories. This is done intentionally, to force them to  keep up and make sure they are paying attention, and also to gently instill a fear of loss.  
  *“Amazon tells you, hour by hour, from one to one million in each category, who is selling the best to the worst. There is no guesswork involved here—you know up to almost the  minute exactly how well each and every product is doing on Amazon. If you know how to look for the right numbers, what an incredible advantage you can have\!”*  
  *“At the time I took this screenshot, this product—a resistance  band set—was the fifty-fourth best seller in the entirety of the Sports and Outdoors category. Having done this for a while, I know this easily translates into 200-plus sales a day, and during times like Christmas and Prime Day, they’re moving 300 or more units per day on autopilot. You know what this is? This is one product doing over one million dollars in sales a year, year in and year out.”*  
  I’m setting up the offer subtly. How can I correlate the best-seller rank with units per day? I expand on that over additional slides, but still leave some back to foster demand.   
  I call this persuasional foreplay. I expand on it on the next slide (figure 37), as I say:  
  *“The clearer you understand what the product you sell on Amazon can do for your life, the more likely you’ll meet with quick success. This is a Tesla, and I own a Tesla. I’ve driven some of the finest automobiles over the years, and this is by far my favorite. It’s my dream car. The monthly payment on this car is exactly $1,486.50. What types of Amazon products would pay for a Tesla?”*  
  …while I explain:  
  *“A lot of product selection research just comes from using the right tools. This is Sellics, a little-known Amazon tool that most sellers have not and will never hear of. It’s an expensive tool, but it’s worth every penny. In less than five minutes, without really even trying, I found several “Tesla” products.*   
  *For example, here is a floor mat. It has a best-seller rank of 1,795, a rating of just 3.9 stars. (The average product on Amazon is rated at 4.4, by the way.) It only has twenty-five reviews. Yet in spite of that, it pulls in around fifteen sales a day. That’s $159 per day. Let’s assume a lower-than-normal profit margin of 40 percent, and this thing can make you, without much effort, $1,908 cash in your pocket—month in and month out. In other words, your dream car plus $500 left over to do with as you please. Now take a look at this product, silicone skins for a camera. It retails for $24.99, and if you look close, you can see it has exactly zero reviews.*   
  *Not a single review. Yet it still sells around seven a day, which translates to $1,872 a month. You might wonder, ‘Jason, why would people buy products without reviews?’ and the answer is simple. To most shoppers on Amazon, the worst product is better than no product. I’m telling you, the Amazon customer is a special beast: many of them will buy practically anything put in front of them\! This is one of the reasons why people succeed in doing their Amazon business with us even if they’ve failed in every previous business endeavor they have tried…”*  
  I continue on like this with the next three products.  
  *“This is not my home, but it’s about fifteen minutes away from where I live. Now, I live in Southern California where the prices are much higher than most other places. Here is a million-dollar home. In Iowa, you’d get a whole lot more home than this for a mil, but even in Southern California this is about 4,000 square feet, ve bedrooms, three baths, and about $5,000 a month for the mortgage. What products could cover your dream home?”*  
  The two biggest purchases most people will ever make in their life are their home and their vehicle. This is why I often use them as examples in my webinars. (Understanding deep primal needs and wants)   
  Repetition of key points is important. People consciously forget most of what they hear, just like most people don’t remember what they ate for dinner twelve days ago. Heck, I even call my cats by my kids’ names and vice versa sometimes\!  
  Use repetition for those key, paradigm-shifting lessons. Just make sure it’s engaging and not boring when you use repetition.  
  With figure 40, I’ve created an objection—intentionally. The objection is:  
  “Jason, I don’t have access to a tool like this.” In their mind, they realize they have to buy it or hope to find a free alternative. During my pitch, though, much to their delight, they’ve discovered I’ve given them full access to Sellics for free, as a bonus. Persuasional foreplay.  
  For the Amazon webinar, I used to tell them: “There are free and paid ways to do this. We have access to a tool you can pay for, though later I can show you how to get it for free. That doesn’t matter, what matters right now is understanding how this relates to the bigger picture of measuring demand to pick products...”  
  What I found was, for this specific instance, not letting them know they could get the tool for free—and positioning it as expensive and hard to nd—worked best. That might not work for a different webinar on a different topic. Use these strategies as guidelines and rene based on data and instinct.  
    
  Now that the strategy for step one has been covered, the last thing I have to do is get commitment to doing what I just showed them and acknowledging that what I showed them was incredible and valuable.  
    
  Figure 41 is how I start with getting commitment.  
    
  Figure 41\. Sample slide from sales webinar  
  Keep in mind, I just showed them products that sell three to ten units a day. Small stuff. Now, I kick it up a level by showing them several slides like the one in figure 42\.  
    
  Figure 42\. Sample slide from sales webinar  
  When I show figure 42 I say:

  “When Eric started, he figured ve to eight units a day was good since he had a full-time job, and oops...he’s selling forty-three units a day.”

  Then I show a slide with Helen, who is doing £6,261.18 within her first thirty days on Amazon, and I say:

  “Here’s Helen, who got up to sixteen units per day in her first thirty days, and she’s not even using Amazon.com—instead selling on the UK Amazon site, which is much smaller, yet is easily bringing her sixteen units a day as she warms up\!”

  I proceed like this with a few more examples of people who started out wanting to go small and end up going big.


  Note the double duty of the Helen testimonial. Not only is she proving my point that people understand Amazon demand, but she’s also international. About 30 percent

  of my audience is from outside of the United States.


  Now that my point is made, it’s time to get commitment, which I do with figure 43\.


  Note that it’s three questions, all with the answer yes. Yes, yes, and yes. I love using the triple yes technique to get commitment.


  Now, I don’t put this on the slide in figure 43, but I say after

  the third bullet point:

  “So, when are you going to start?” Pause. “If you didn’t answer,

  ‘As soon as humanly possible,’ check your pulse to make sure you’re still alive\!”

    
  When you start, it’s recommended that you just flat out write on the slide what you want them to commit to and simply read it out loud to them. Once you get a knack

  for it, though, you’ll find sometimes it’s better to make it feel organic by saying it out loud, seemingly on the top of your head.


  And say:

  “Now that you have that perfect product to start your Amazon business, it’s time to source it, then list and launch it. Let’s talk about sourcing.”

  Simple transition. Note that I phrased it as if they have already done it. This creates ownership, which makes it easier to get them to buy the product you sell at the end.


  

* ### **Commitment:** 

  Get the audience to promise to take action.    
  Then you get commitment and say things like now that you understand step one…   
  Are you willing to put it into action?  
  It’s not enough to just teach somebody you also need to get them committed

	TYPES OF COMMITMENTS

As we’ve discussed in the introduction section, there are macro-commitments and micro-commitments. These can be applied either directly or indirectly.

If you do nothing else, adding direct micro-commitments to your webinar presentations should add a significant amount of selling power to them.

A micro-commitment is designed to get a yes from your audience. I like to get 150 yeses before I ever ask for the order.

In fact, let’s take that one sentence and turn it into a micro-commitment. Getting more yeses before you ask for a “yes” decision related to your offer would go a long way, wouldn’t

it? And isn’t it simple, if you think about it, to get these micro-commitments? When you get these commitments, doesn’t

it make sense to do it in the most natural way possible?

Let’s analyze. Wouldn’t it? Isn’t it? Doesn’t it? At the beginning of the sentence, in the middle of the sentence, at the end of it.

You have to get good at mixing up the specific commitment phrases as well as the positioning them, otherwise it can get distracting...can’t it?

Indeed. This will feel awkward at first, won’t it? Isn’t it unnatural? Because this takes practice, doesn’t it make sense to have some go-to phrases you can develop to always fall back on?

Again, notice I used one commitment at the beginning, another in the middle, and yet another at the end. Make sense?

“Make sense?” is yet another commitment phrase. You’d like to know the one I use most often though...right?

“Right?” is actually my favorite because it’s one word and you can stick at on the end of any sentence (right?).

Here are other similar commitment phrases to “right”:

Agreed? Correct? Deal? See what I mean? Understood? Got it?

There are also soft commitments. You can phrase any commitment as either hard or soft. Compare “Is it starting to become clear to you?” versus “It’s becoming clear to you, isn’t it?”

“Does that make sense?” versus “Doesn’t that make sense?”

“Does that ring true with you?” versus “That rings true with you, doesn’t it?”

“Is it beginning to fall in place?” versus “It’s beginning to fall in place, isn’t it?”

Mostly, you want to use hard commitments. Most presenters talk at their audience but don’t talk to their audience. Hard commitments are a way to check in with your audience to make sure they’re in sync with you.

There are times, though, where you should use soft commitments. Either for effect or because you truly aren’t sure if your audience got what you just said.

*“Are we on the same page?”*  

I’ll sometimes ask after going through a step to see if the audience “got it” or not. If they didn’t get it, I don’t pretend they did. I address it. 

Example:

*“Okay, for some of you it isn’t clear yet, but I think it will become clear to you over the next few slides. So even if it doesn’t make sense right now, it should become apparent as we move forward.”*

Sometimes, I can tell I lost the audience completely, so I

will oat out say something like:

*“Okay, I screwed up explaining that, because if you got what I just said, I think you’d be much more excited than you are. So let me try that again.”*

Then I will verbally go through, on the oy, what I think is a better explanation and get commitment for that before moving on. Afterwards, I’ll x my webinar so that doesn’t happen again\!

You can and should also use certain, specific soft commitments for flair. Here are some of the ones I use to really add a punch to my presentations:

*“If we stopped the webinar right now, would you feel you’ve already gotten more from this webinar than most if not all other webinars you’ve attended?”* Pause for answer. 

*“Excellent. And here’s the thing. We’re just getting started.”*

Another:

“Do you think that doing this instead of what you’re currently doing is likely to yield a better result? Are you willing to promise me that you’ll do this instead the next time the situation comes up? Swear? Pinky promise?”

Another:

“Now, you have one of three choices. You can choose to do things the old way—the natural way, but the limiting way nonetheless. I call this maintaining the status quo. Your second choice is to do nothing. Not sure how that’s going to help you, but it is a choice. Your third option—you can actually use what I showed you. Not think about it, not just say ‘Yeah, that sounds like a good idea,’ but actually take this thing out in the real world and make it show up where it counts. Which of these three options can you see yourself doing?”

I like to, throughout the presentation, have three or four of these commitments, because they place the emphasis on action, not just on learning.

You should begin to construct your set of macro commitments that you can whip out and use as easily and naturally as breathing. I scripted and memorized mine when I first started until it became second nature.

Again, feel free to use as much of the material in this book in your presentations as you wish. Borrow phrases liberally.

Here is a formula you can use as well to make this a snap for creating your own commitment scripts. I call it the “one, two, three commitment formula.” You ask a broad commitment question, a specific commitment question, and then the question that gets the big commitment.

Here is one of the simplest ones to use to transition from content to pitch:

• Broad commitment question: “Did you enjoy our time together on the webinar thus far?” Yes.

• Specific commitment question: “Would you like to spend more time together than just this one webinar?” Yes.

• Big commitment question: “If I had something that would take what we discussed today and kick it up to the next level, would you like to know about it?” Yes.

Another example:  
“You can see how this could save you a lot of time and money, right?” Yes. “And saving a bunch of time and money would make a huge impact on your life, wouldn’t it?” Yes. “So what  
I just showed you—which we agreed is valuable both in the time and the money department—instead of wasting it, are you actually going to commit to me, yourself, and the whole world to use it?”

One more example:  
“Wouldn’t it have been nice to know this twenty years ago instead of just now?” Yes. “And doesn’t it suck that most people will go their whole life blissfully unaware of this?”

Yes. “Yet even if you knew this twenty years ago and chose to ignore it, you’d actually be worse off today than remaining in the darkness of your own ignorance because you willingly  
played a role in your own downfall. What would you need to do to make sure this doesn’t happen?”

One more thing on commitments—if done wrong, it’s annoying. I still, to this very day, see speakers who should know better than to say dumb stuff on webinars like, “Who here wants more money?” Blah. Not only is it completely unimaginative, but the audience feels manipulated. Despite that, commitments are so powerful that even being a hack about it can work. However, I prefer to not annoy the audience while getting commitment.  
Instead of saying, “Who here wants more money?” you could say, “Wouldn’t it be nice if more money showed up in your life more often?” This commitment phrase accomplishes  
the same result, yet it’s put forth in a much more palatable way. Instead of, “Who here wants more money?” they could say, “I’m going to make an assumption that you want to get  
unreasonably wealthy in an unreasonable amount of time.  
Is my assumption correct?” The point is don’t be lazy with your commitments.  
What I recommend you do is get your webinar transcribed and go through it with a ne-toothed comb to see where you are asking for commitments and how you’re asking. I bet you’ll be shocked at how little commitment elicitation you’re performing—which is scary, because commitments are fundamental to all selling, not just webinars.

## **Transition (3-5 minutes)**

The transition section is designed to bridge the gap between the content and the close. It should include elements such as:  

### **60 Second Recap:** 

Summarize the key points of your presentation.  

Look what are the most cool and amazing insights strategies, aha moments I’ve shared in the Content Section… How can I remind the audience of all the awesomeness in 60 seconds or less? 

So far today you discovered how to do …blank\_\_\_ the insight over there…. This cool strategy on\_\_\_ This thing over here and this thing and this thing and this thing… 

You do it really rapidly with a ton of enthusiasm so that people are like OMG that was a ton of value\! And also you are reminded like OMG I gave a ton of value. 

And then you switch to the

* ### **Yes Momentum:** 

  Ask the audience a series of questions that will get them to say "yes” to a better tomorrow… Was our time well spent together? Did you learn something that you didn’t expect to learn? Can you see yourself rightnow succeeding when you were previously failing? Are you glad that you came here? Are you eager to get started? 

* ### **Two Choices:**

   Give the audience the choice to either do it on their own or do it with your help.   
  So now I’m faced with a decision do you I’ll leave all dressed up and excited and send you on your way and hope that you make the best of it? And just (sigh) Leave  you be??

  That’s an Option or The Second Option is that I could provide to you all the best resources and could create Support, Community and Accountability for you and give you some shortcuts. Which Option would you prefer? 

  When it comes to BLANK, I know you better than you know yourself… (You should know your customer better than yourself when it comes to a particular problem) …  
  If left in your own devices here’s what is going to happen… You’re going to be excited about this temporarily, and you’ll think you’re going to change the world and then LIFE is GOING TO INTERRUPT YOU as it does every time… Limiting Belief are going to try to interrupt you. And six months from now if I run into you, I’ll say how you’re doing with this you’ll say, I’m still where I’m at. That’s a tragedy\! Now what you must think on some creative new ways of making a permanent change in your business and I have one idea for today, invest on making yourself the best realtor of your city. Invest on a strategy that will make you rich.  
    
  With great pleasure I would like to introduce to you… (The Offer)

  \#\#\#

  Example: 

  On the webinar with webinars, with slides flying, I’d say something like this:  
  “In our brief time together today, I’ve given you the exact formula I’ve spent years perfecting to the tune of nine figures.

  You now immediately possess it, and with it, all the power it holds. You now know how to, in the first ve minutes, get more people wanting to buy from you than most webinars get for the whole entire webinar. You have certain webinar ‘magic tricks’ to practically manifest conversion and prot, almost out of thin air. I’ve given you a process for sharing your content in a way that creates commitment in your audience so it’s harder to say ‘no’ to your offer at the end than just simply saying ‘yes.’ You have the approach that not only makes the sale of the product today, but sells the  
  audience on you so they are more likely to buy from you in the future, buy more often with less resistance, and buy at higher prices. You discovered the ve-part pitch formula to make selling pretty much a ‘paint-by-numbers exercise,’ and as a result, you’ll be able to make more sales moving forward than you’ve ever made in your life. I’ve given you the confidence to transition from educating to selling, even if you hate selling. I’ve sprinkled in tactics, tricks, and near effortless things you can immediately use that, simple as they are to implement, can have a profound impact on your results and your bank account. All this and much, much more in the limited time we had to interact together today...”  
  The “half-dozen yeses” technique is a series of questions—six in total—to get your audience in an agreeable state, which will make them more likely to say “yes” to your offer.  
  Here’s an example from the webinar on webinars:  
  “Knowing what you now know...  
    
  1\. Do you feel more comfortable harnessing the power of webinars in your business?  
  2\. Were you happy you came to the webinar today?  
  3\. Do you realize the advantage you have in the market by using these cutting-edge webinar techniques?  
  4\. Can you see yourself using what I showed you today to help you grow your business?  
  5\. Even if you use just a tiny fraction of what I showed you, would you say our time was well spent?  
  6\. Would you like to spend even more time together, going even deeper and further on how to make webinars show up in your business with impact?”  
    
  I call this “yes momentum.” Getting six yeses directly before going into the pitch can do wonders for your sales conversions.   
  There’s just one more thing you now have to do to complete your transition. I call this “the two choices.”  
    
  **THE TWO CHOICES**  
  Here’s the template I created for this:  
  “Now, here’s what I know about you. Even if we had four hours together instead of just forty-ve minutes, it’s going to be hard—almost impossible—to create lasting change, to give you the full extent and benet of all that I could give you. No matter how good anyone is—and I’m better than most—one measly webinar isn’t really going to go about creating the change in your life that you want and deserve. You need more than that. While what I’ve given you today was incredibly valuable, as you have told me, it’s frankly the tip of the iceberg. And if you like what I’ve shared with  
  you so far, you’ll love what I’ve got for you next if you said to yourself that you want to go even further than our brief encounter today. You see, before doing this webinar today, I was faced with one of two choices. The first choice is I could share what I’ve shared thus far, part ways with you, and then hope that on your own you can make a go of it and maybe be successful. Or my second option is I could take a more active role and responsibility for your success, to create a situation where our relationship could evolve from a one-and-done type of deal to an ongoing, growing, and mutually-rewarding relationship—one where I would do everything I could to make your success certain. I choose the second option, and when you see what I have in store for you, you’ll be glad that I did. It is with great pleasure to introduce to you...”  
  Then you reveal the product name, and this marks the end of the transition section.  
  Let’s break down the technique of the “two choices” transition.  
  First, we acknowledge reality—big change usually comes from repeated exposure over a period of time, not just one time. This is logical and applicable to pretty much anything you’re going to pitch, which is why I use it frequently in my  
  Transition. Second, “...you need more than that.” I’m positioning what I’m about to sell as something of great benefit to them. Third, “And if you like what I’ve shared with you so far, you’ll love what I’ve got for you next...” This is called linking. I’m connecting a statement of truth with one that has yet to be proven. I learned this through studying hypnosis. Fact. Fact.  
    
  Opinion. Fact. Fact. Claim. You’re a living, breathing human being (fact). You face challenges and you face opportunities each and every day (fact). Now, you’re going to be able to get more out of the opportunities you have and turn your challenges into your greatest strengths (claim). By setting up your claim with one or two facts directly preceding it, your claim is more easily acceptable.  
  Fourth, “Before doing this webinar today, I was faced with one of two choices.” This is actually a logical fallacy, technically called a “false dilemma.” I was faced with far more than two choices. Yet we employ it because it helps us control the focus on the conversation to make it as black and white as possible, between the bad of not offering them something versus the good of offering it to them.  
  Fifth, “I choose the second option, and when you see what I have in store for you, you’ll be glad that I did...” Positioning what you’re about to sell to them as a favor, a good thing—not as something evil, which is how most people superficially  
  view selling.  
  Now we head into the close, with both you and the audience ready to make something wonderful happen.  
  


  ## **Close (45+ minutes)**

  The close is where you make your offer and ask for the sale. It should include elements such as:    
* Offer: Clearly state the name of your product or service, its benefits, and its price.    
  We give them all the details and the core part of what they are expecting to buy…out of the way as quickly as possible so we can do our first close. Knowing well that most people are going to say no the first time they see something. 

  We are anchoring PRICE to the Core offer…Here what it is, here what it does, here is how you get access to it…

  THEN YOU want to start revealing the PRICE so in the right hand is worth blank… What is worth? Well for me it was worth 100.000.000 dollars… and  for people like John Clayton that I thought this to this is worth several million dollars in their businesses … People have paid $5000 to sit in on a seminar where I trained on this exact formula over two days… If you go to the public Website the price is $2000 however if you get started today the price is $1499… Go to example.com right now to get started…

  And now people know the Price… They know it’s a limited time price… You always need to give your webinars attendees a Special Deal… 

   and then we are going to STACK BONUSES… STACK VALUE and STACK VALUE...  
    
* Bonuses: Offer additional bonuses to sweeten the deal.    
  And when you act before the countdown time expires as an extra special bonus here’s what you get for FREE:   
  The name of the Bonus  
  Why it’s an awesome bonus, why you included it…  
  Some of the cool things and the Proof that make this bonus an amazing bonus and you add a call to action…  
  And go here now and sign up before this offer expires etc…  
  Also when you sign up you will get BONUS number 2  
  And you this on with the other bonuses  
* Guarantee: Reverse the risk or turn it into a benefit.    
* Objections: Address any remaining objections the audience may have.    
* Scarcity: Create a sense of urgency by emphasizing the limited-time nature of the offer.   


### **THE OFFER**

Here’s where it gets interesting: the offer is the least important part of the close. Most presenters think it’s the most important, and it shows. They spend so much time discussing every little detail of what’s in the offer that the audience ends up being bored. It’s hard to bore someone into buying.

Another problem with the offer portion is that presenters tend to focus too much on the features of the offers, not the benefits. They sell you the drill (feature), but what you really want is the hole the drill makes (benet). Everything they get in your offer are the features of the offer. What it can do for them are the benefits.

I wish I could skip the offer section together and focus just on benefits, but people need to justify their purchase logically, so they need to be able to clearly understand what it is they

spent their money on. We give them just enough of the features of the offer to satisfy and make them feel comfortable, while setting up the real, powerful emotional states that lead to purchases. That’s why you want to spend the least amount of time on your “offer” section as possible. I typically spend about three to five minutes and follow this flow:

• Product name and tagline

• One-sentence benefit statement

• Highlight the major components

If it takes longer than ve minutes to do this, I’ve highlighted more than the major components of the offer. If it takes less than three minutes to do this, then my ofer isn’t strong enough and I know I’ll need to punch it up.

PRODUCT NAME AND TAGLINE

For my webinar on webinars, I pitch a product called Genius Webinars. The tagline to it is “Secrets of $100,000,000+ in webinar sales.” That’s it\! Part one of the offer flow has been accomplished.

Another product I’ve sold really well on webinars was called Product eClass.

Easy to say and remember. Sounds cool. Here’s where it gets even more interesting—it’s intentionally low key.

Why? Because the audiences I was reaching at the time were typically exposed to offers that were hyped. While my competition would be using names like “Product Money

Makers,” “Info Product Riches,” “Million Dollar Info Product,” etc. I chose to stand out by contrast. If I were in a market that was mostly low key, then a little bit of hype could go a long way.

The second part is the tagline. Usually, this is an indirect benet. In my case—“Secrets of $100,000,000+ in webinar sales”—the implication is that once you learn these secrets, you can make a lot of money, too. A less-indirect tagline would be: “Unlocking the true wealth that exists in your webinars.” A super-direct tagline would be: “How to create webinars that make you rich.” Sometimes, it’s a matter of taste how much hype you want to put into your tagline.

Remember, the approach goes: product name, tagline, and then benet statement. I like to go from subtle (product name), to less subtle (tagline), to not subtle at all.

ONE-SENTENCE BENEFIT STATEMENT

The goal of the benet statement is to encapsulate in one sentence the totality of the benefit available in your offer.

Not an easy task\!

For Genius Webinars, this is the benet statement I use: “A step-by-step approach for crafting webinars that outsell your competition; provide more value to your customers; and are easier, quicker, and more enjoyable to create than you thought even possible.”

I’m a firm believer in using both direct and indirect means to make a point. See the progression:

Title: Genius Webinars

Tagline: Secrets of $100,000,000+ in webinar sales.

Benet statement: A step-by-step approach for crafting webinars that outsell your competition; provide more value to your customers; and are easier, quicker, and more enjoyable to create than you thought even possible.”

I will accomplish those three things over two or three slides. The benet statement should be all about what’s in it for them. In that one sentence, here are the benefits I packed

into it:

• Outsell your competition

• Provide more value to your customer

• Easier

• Quicker

• More enjoyable

Five benefits. Most people are lucky to come up with more than one when introducing the offer.

Until this becomes second nature to you, I suggest you actually write it down word for word on your slide and read it to your audience word for word. This allows you to clearly articulate in one single sentence the essence of your offer and the power it provides for the audience.

HIGHLIGHT MAJOR COMPONENTS

First, we have to figure out what the major components of the offer are. To do this, you should list every deliverable they get in full when they sign up.

For the webinar on webinars, here is what I came up with while first crafting my offer section:

• Two-day, in-o¦ce training at the Genius Network headquarters

• Full, professional recordings of the onsite training

• World-class service and experience

• Big book of webinar closes

• Webinar funnels (registration, thank-you pages, order

forms, etc.)

• Worksheets, checklists, and templates

• Free consulting on your webinar pitch once completed

Once you list out all the components, then you have to decide what should go into the main offer and what you’ll hold back for the bonuses.

What makes something better as a bonus than a main offer?

The first is the “wow” factor. Something that would blow their mind when you reveal it should, if possible, be reserved as a bonus. Another reason you’d put something as a bonus is if it’s “thin.” What I mean by that is, while it may have a lot of benet, if it doesn’t take much to consume it, it’s better as a bonus than part of the main offer. If it’s obvious that it should be part of the main offer, then it shouldn’t be made a bonus.

Everything else you just use your best judgment on where you think it should land. We’ll talk more specifically about the bonus portion of the close section later. But just know that I want to see at least three bonuses, but ideally ve bonuses.  
Also remember that you don’t want to spend more than ve minutes in the offer section either.

The first was obvious—that is the main appeal of what they get—in person training with me for two days to cover the ins and outs of the webinar process. The second is important, but doesn’t do a whole lot to sell the product. That’s why I make it part of the offer and not a bonus. People expect great service, but we’re going to let them know just how great it will be. The third thing I felt made more sense in the offer because I can easily tie it into the two-day live training.

This is where “*how”* we highlight the major components of your offer comes into play. The formula we use here is:

• Sexy headline

• Feature-plus-benet bullets (three to four)

• Future pace

• Proof

For Genius Webinars, the first component is the two-day, in-office training at the Genius Network headquarters. I could use that as a headline, or I could punch it up and make it sound more exciting (aka “sexy”).

Example: “Live, real-time training for complete webinar mastery\!” There, much better.

Now, the “feature-plus-benet bullets.” We want to create three or four bullets that show off the more valuable parts of that major component. The first part of the bullet is “what it is,” and the second part is “what it can do for you.” Examples:

• “A full-sensory experience of creating your own million-dollar webinars; see it, hear it and feel it in a safe, intimate, closed-door environment, where over two days you get the total extent of Jason’s webinar expertise, so it can show up in a big way in your business.

• Each session over this two-day, live coaching is structured in a way that will automatically turn ideas into implementation in real time so that you don’t leave with just a bunch of notes, you leave with something that can move the world.

• You’ll be surrounded by the best of the best in business, and we will help and encourage each other to make the world a better place with the webinars we create together in the room\!

Next, “future pace”—explain on a single slide what life is going be like for them once they master this skill. Example:

“Now, any time a great opportunity presents itself where you know a webinar is just the thing for it, you’ll leap into action with a newfound sense of confidence, knowing full well your promotions have more oomph, more impact on your customers, and more impact on your bottom line.”

Lastly, “proof.” This includes your own results, other people’s results, testimonials, or statements of fact. If possible,

I prefer other people’s results who directly went through that portion of the offer. If that doesn’t exist, then I like a customer testimonial about how effective I am related to that particular part of the offer. If I don’t have that and can’t get it before the webinar, then I will share my own results as it relates to that component. If there isn’t an easy way I can show that, then I’ll use statements of fact. That’s what I did the first time we ever offered Genius Network: “Joe only

makes his o¦ce available for the best in the world to come

in and use, and this is the first time he has ever promoted

to his whole entire audience something like this, so you can

imagine how incredible it’s going to be\!”

That’s okay. I’d have much rather preferred having someone who has gone through it in the past say, *“I’ve been to Joe’s office several times, but this was the most valuable time I ever spent at Genius headquarters, by far. I made just one change, based on something Jason said after lunch the first day, that made me over $150,000 in extra money on a webinar I had all but given up on.”*

Yet, any proof is better than no proof.

If you put it all together, the headline should show up at the

top of your slide. Each bullet point should be its own slide,

written word-for-word exactly how you will say it, with the

sexy headline at the top of each bullet. Then you have one

slide for the future-pacing statement and one final slide for

proof. You’re looking at either ve or six slides there, and

if you spend twenty seconds per slide, just one component

is going to take you about two minutes to explain. You can

see how easy it is to get carried away with the offer section.

You usually want to blast through this as fast as you can, and

often twenty seconds per slide is too long\! I like slides that I

can blaze through in ten to fifteen seconds. Bonus points if

you can add a strong visual as you introduce the main com-

ponent. In this case, I could have a great image of Joe’s office

and people in it having a good time to give them something

concrete to associate with this component.

If you didn’t quite get how to do it off of the one example I

gave, fear not—we’ll spend a lot more time on this formula

because, conveniently, it’s exactly how we reveal bonuses

as well—which we’ll cover after we...

### **REVEAL PRICE**

The price tag gets in the way of every consumer—you, me,

and our respective audiences. I’m sure you’ve heard the

phrase “You get what you pay for.” Oh, only if that were

true\! Then, if we wanted the best, we’d simply look at the

offer that was most expensive.

Yet price serves a utility of acting as “shorthand” to help a consumer decide if something is a good deal or not. Until you reveal the price, the customer can’t quite understand

how valuable your offer is as it relates to them.

This is one of the main reasons we like to get price out of the way as soon as possible. Most presenters take far too long to reveal price, and it causes distractions. The more you go on about what they get without them knowing how much they must pay to get it, the less likely they are to pay attention to and understand the value of what they do get.

There is another psychological reason I like to reveal the price within the first ve minutes of introducing the offer: most people are unlikely to say “yes” the first time they are presented with a major investment and opportunity for change.

Sales studies have shown that, in the past, it took seven times of asking for an order before the average person would say “yes.” That meant six noes\! I think that data is not current, either; in my experience, I aim for twenty-six times. I won’t give up on a sale until I ask for the order twenty-six times\!

Naturally, you can’t ask for the order until they know “how much.” Since they are likely to say no the first time anyway,

let’s let them get it out of their system quickly, without them even knowing the full extent of what they’re getting. They say “no” with limited information, then with each new piece of information we provide them with, it presents a new opportunity to ask them to say “yes.”

When I reveal the price, I first link it to a much higher price point, then I stair step it down to the special pricing.

LINK TO A HIGHER PRICE POINT

An example from the webinar on webinars:

“Listen, the type of information I first shared is just a small portion of what Genius X members get, which is Joe’s highest level mastermind that brings with it a $100,000 price tag.

And you’ve seen that this has produced over $10,000,000 in sales from one campaign. If I were to price this at what it is truly worth, I wouldn’t have any issue asking you to invest $100,000 to join Genius Webinars right here and right now.” I’ve positioned my product, which I will sell for $4,997, to be on pace with a $100,000 investment. This was done by linking it to something that actually costs that much. If I didn’t have that going for me, I could’ve just as easily said,

“As you can see, this stuff has generated tens of millions for me and my clients, and any sane, rational entrepreneur would easily put $100,000 down today if it meant one million dollars or more in the near future. For many people,

$100,000 would be an easy decision to make to get started with Genius Webinars...”

If you don’t have such a direct comparison to price or results, you can do it indirectly. If I were selling a weight loss program, I could easily do something like this:

“As I showed you earlier, studies show that you live ten or more years if you lead a healthy and active lifestyle. I know without a shadow of a doubt that once you get your hands on this program, you’ll not only feel better, but you’ll feel better longer. How much would you pay to add an extra ten years to your life? Many people would spend $25,000 or more for ten years of the same quality of life they currently have, not to speak of the tremendously-improved quality of life you’ll soon be enjoying...”

STAIR-STEP DOWN TO THE RIDICULOUS

We want to amplify the feeling of the deal that the audience is getting, so we don’t immediately go from the high value to price link we’ve established immediately to the actual price of the product.

For Genius Webinars, we started at $100,000, and before we get to the $4,997 price point, I’m going to stair step them down to $25,000 and $10,000 before revealing the actual price.

Example:

“Even though $100,000 for this can easily be justified, I’m in the business of making deals so unfavorably in my customer’s advantage that it’s silly. To be part of Genius Network itself the price tag is $25,000, and they don’t let anyone with a

pulse and a $25,000 check in the door, either. Many people happily pay Joe $25,000 per year because they know that one single connection is worth many times that $25,000 investment. How many more connections do you think you can make when you start doing  million-dollar webinars? At $25,000 straight up, it should be obvious to you that you’re getting the better end of the deal here.”

Now, the next step down. “Yet we can do better. Joe’s annual event, done once a year, is $10,000 for two days, over 1,000 people apply to come, and only 300 get accepted. So therefore, that’s what makes sense for me to offer Genius Webinars for—a one-time invest- ment of just $10,000 for the ability to create far more than that each and every time you use Genius Webinars in your business.”

Then I pause for dramatic effect before continuing. “Better still—I’ve decided to reward those who act boldly and immediately because those are the type of people I love to

do business with. If you sign up within the next forty-eight hours, instead of $10,000—which is truly already such a good price it’s ridiculous—you’ll be able to get full access to everything that makes up this wonderful program called

Genius Webinars for—get this—just $4,997 when you go to \[URL\].”

The lesson is that price is relative. People cannot imagine numbers in their minds so easily once you get past what you can count on your hands and toes. They need to compare them to things they can more easily wrap their mind around. In this case, we control what it can be compared to, and then we create excitement by making something great appear greater...then greater, then greater still\! If I were to come out and just say, “It’s $4,997,” people would get sticker shock\!

Lastly, dress it up. Add flair to it. Pregnant pauses. Make it dramatic. The more of this you do, the more eager your audience will be to say “yes” to the offer.

With that said, I still go into this first price reveal with the mentality that most people won’t buy. The higher the price, the more likely that is to be true, too. Even if it’s not true, it puts you in the right state of mind to have your webinars perform at the highest level possible.

This is why as soon as we reveal price and tell them where to go to buy (the first true close), we immediately switch the focus back to value.

You do this with...

### **THE BONUSES**

Before you ever write your close section, you should have a firm understanding of what your whole offer is in its entirety, and which parts of your offer will be main components and which parts will be the bonuses.

Not only that, but you should have an idea of what your best two bonuses are so that you can lead with the second-best

bonus and save the best bonus for last.

What’s interesting is that, if you were to analyze how much time you spent on a webinar talking about the core offer versus how much time you spend on the bonuses, you’d discover you usually spend two to three times longer on the bonuses if you’re using my approach. That’s by design.

It doesn’t make sense on the surface to focus more on the extras than on the main attraction, but it makes all the sense in the world when it comes to selling.

What we’ve done up to this point is linked the price they pay with the core offer. Likely, they are now in a “maybe” state.

They can see the value in the offer, they can appreciate that it is a good deal, and they are now wrestling with if they should or shouldn’t go forward with it. They are already close to a yes based on the information that is currently available to them. Imagine the effect it has on them when you keep adding even better stuff, for “free,” that they can get on top of what they are already getting. This short-circuits their excitement, which is a stronger force for purchasing than all the logic in the world.

How we present our bonuses largely follows the same

formula:

• Sexy headline

• Feature-plus-benet bullets (three to four)

• Future pace

• Proof

With just one addition between the headline and bullets, we add a “context” section.

First, we provide context as to why this bonus is so valuable. I do this by showing them how important it is to have captured the whole event in its entirety.

Second, notice the URL at the bottom of the slide. Most of the slides I’ll show once I reveal the price will now have the URL of where to sign up for my o¥er, so there is never any doubt of how to buy. You go to the URL on the slide. What slide? Pretty much every slide from here on out\! Now, we proceed as normal, with feature-plus-benet bullets.

Here are the ones I used for this bonus:

• We’re going to put Joe’s $125,000+ worth of recording equipment to good use, capturing all the wonderful content as professionally as anyone in the business could.

• Every session in its entirety will be recorded and organized in a way that you can nd exactly what you need later, effortlessly.

• I don’t know what we’re going to do with these recordings in the future—we might hoard them or keep them exclusive.

If we do offer them, it will be for major $$$. You get it FOR FREE.

Next, future pace and/or proof. You don’t always have to use both, but I try to as much as possible, especially for the big bonuses (the first bonus and the last bonus).

A future-pace slide for this bonus could be: “Now, whenever you want, on any device you wish to, you can view the best webinar advice, technique, and insight in the world on demand...”

I could combine this with “proof ” being an image of the DVDs laid out attractively in a way that makes the audience say to themselves, “I want those\!”

It’s important to remember that the formula should be used as a guide and not something that is inflexible and must be followed exactly.

The first slide gives the headline and sets the context. Then, for this bonus, I think it’s important to spend a little more time on context, so figure 57 is the next slide I use.

This should be done for bonuses that aren’t obvious to the audience how valuable they are.

Then I follow it up with bullet points:

• You get the full webinar funnel, from registration to replay to sign-up page, so you can take these plug-and-play templates and drop the perfect webinar funnel into your promotions in seconds.

• In fact, there are two major secret weapons I use in my funnels that I am not going to disclose here, but you will get them and understand immediately how insanely powerful they are for your business\!

Notice the second bullet where I create an open loop that is only closed by purchasing. I like to have one of my bonuses do that to give my close some extra repower. Here, I only used two bullets instead of three, and I did so because I spent a little extra time on the context and didn’t want to disrupt my flow.

One thing to remember about bonuses is that they can be shaped to specifically counter objections. In fact, the first bonus counters the objection about “What if I miss something while I’m there?” The second bonus counters the “I have my webinar, but now what?” objection. This third bonus counters the “I don’t want to have to wait a long time to see a return on my investment” objection, as well as all the little minor things like, “What should I use for my webinar? How do I set my webinar up?” etc.

“In addition to getting the top-quality recordings of each and every live session you attend, plus this webinar funnel that can easily double the profits of any webinar, you’ll also get

everything you need before coming to the Genius Webinar training to ensure your success.”

Notice how, when I compounded the bonuses this time, I highlighted the bonuses slightly differently than the last time? I do this each time I compound. Reveal a bonus. Review

all bonuses to that point. Reveal another bonus. Review all bonuses up to this point in a slightly different fashion. Repeat.

Also, when introducing each bonus, I like to say, “When you sign up at \[URL\], you’re also going to get this\!” or “To get your hands on this bonus, simply go to \[URL\] to get started right now,” and so on. I’m always, as naturally as possible, working in calls to actions to get them to go and buy.

You should, if possible, save your best bonus for last. When you compound your bonuses, you can then say, before revealing this last bonus, “And I’ve saved the best for last. When you sign up at \[URL\] today, you’re also going to get...in addition to… \[review all bonuses again\]...and this...”

In this case, the best bonus I have for Genius Webinars is personal consulting with me (figure 62).

You save the best bonus for last, because this gives you the extra push to knock them off the fence and into buying territory. Chances are, they were already getting ready to buy anyway, or they were this-close to buying, and when you have that last, best trick up your sleeve, this ultimate bonus—game over.

The reason this works so well is that most presenters don’t have the nerve to hold back like this. It’s a lack of confidence.

They are so scared of rejection and missing the sale that they lead with the best thing they can right up front, and when the person says no—which they will likely do no matter what—it’s all downhill from there.

Yet if you watch the best movies and TV shows in the world, they build up to the payoff. If you watch the best comedians in the world, they end with their best materials. As a webinar presenter, you should do so as well. Take the best thing you have for making the sale and save it for your last bonus.

Then, boom\!

After revealing your last bonus, do a major call to action.

Something like this: “Open up your favorite browser on your computer right now—whether it’s Internet Explorer, Firefox, Chrome, Safari, whatever—and type in \[URL\]. When you go to that page, I want you to make note of the following...

First, see this countdown timer? When that baby hits zero, you will in fact, miss out on the special pricing, so make sure you sign up as soon as you can.

Second, at the bottom of this page—and all of our pages for that matter—is a link to support. This is where you go if you need anything at any time, and we’ll be glad to assist you.

Now, see this “Add to Cart” button? I want you to click on it. When you do, it will take you to this screen where you can agree to our Terms of Service if they’re to your liking—then

ll out the first part of this acceptance form.

After you ll out the form, click “Checkout with PayPal” and you’ll be taken to this screen that you now see in front of you.

If you wish, you can simply complete your acceptance form by using PayPal. Or if you don’t have PayPal or prefer to use a credit or debit card, then click ‘Don’t have a PayPal

account.’

Regardless of how you decide to invest right now, as soon as you complete your checkout, you’ll get an email from me that looks like this...”

### **THE GUARANTEE**

Even if you do have an unconditional guarantee, it’s advisable to consider adding a conditional guarantee on top of that.

In fact, the best webinar I have ever done in terms of sales

also had the strongest guarantee I’ve ever created—and

what many people call the greatest guarantee of all time.

The profit guarantee.

After revealing all of our bonuses on our Amazon webinar, I transition to the guarantee over a series of slides while saying: “I hope you see how serious we are about this and what it can do for you. So let’s go in all the way together. I’m so condent

in your success, based on our track record and our downright unfair resources only available through the link below, that I can legally guarantee you profits when you sign up. How?

It’s called...THE PROFIT GUARANTEE.”

Next, I set the stage to counteract the objection of “If this thing is so good, why would you need such a grand guarantee anyway?”

“When you sign up today, here’s what will happen. You’ll build a successful business that can easily be turned into a million-dollar-a-year enterprise. If you, for whatever inexplicable reason, don’t create a business within a short timeframe, profiting at a rate of at least $2,500 per month, then you’ll have two options.

Option One: You will refund your purchase of Amazing Selling Machine (ASM), and we will buy your business (including inventory) for double what it cost you to get started, plus give you $5,000 for your time (up to a grand total of $10,000).

Option Two: You will stay in ASM and we will personally help you reach $25,000 in revenue within ninety days. Why do we do this? We do this for a very selfish reason. I’m more than happy to pay your costs and buy your business for up to $10,000. I get the better end of the deal. However, at least this guarantees you profit no matter what. If you don’t want to sell us your business, then I’ll personally help you reach $25,000 in revenue within ninety days. How? I will work with you one to one to make your business successful.

Now what if by some small miracle, with all my help, you still don’t reach $25,000 in ninety days? Then I just hand you over an established Amazon business.”

Then, on the next slides, I say:

“When you sign up, I know for a fact one of these three things will happen: You will be profitable with your own business.

You will get paid up to $10,000 from us to buy your business. You will generate $25,000 in revenue in ninety days or we hand you over an established Amazon business.”

What you do when you offer a guarantee is remove the risk.

The more you can go about removing the risk, the more likely someone is to say “yes” to your offer. After you make your guarantee, end with a strong call to action. Now, it’s objection destruction time.

### **OBJECTIONS**

Here, we return to the big two—which you will always face if you’re selling anything beyond an impulse purchase—time and money.

After you present your guarantee, here is how I usually transition: I reframe them from objections to questions.

“Now, at this point I see a lot of you have signed up, and that makes me happy. Some of you are still here though, and I can tell you’re getting ready to sign up, but you have a question you need answered first before making that decision, so let’s address those questions in the time we have left.”

to sneeze at. However, let’s say if instead

of having to invest $4,997 in this program, you found out

you needed to have a life-saving operation by tomorrow night,

and the price of that operation was $4,997. Would you say,

‘Oh, I can’t afford that, I’ll just die?’ Of course not. So let’s

get rid of the myth of whether you can or can’t afford it. The

real question is, are you willing to do what it takes to make

this investment or not? As you sit here today, you have three

options. Option one is to do nothing, and Aristotle put it best:

“Say nothing, do nothing, be nothing.” Doing nothing just

doesn’t leave you with the problem, it makes the problem worse the longer you do nothing. So that’s not it. You can do

something else, but why? You know and I know that what

is right in front of you is the thing to do. And that’s option

number three—just do it. Yes, the money may be tight. Yes,

this may be a stretch. Yes, you’re going to have to go out of

your comfort zone a bit. Where do you think all the growth

will come from? That’s why you need to quit lying to me

(and more importantly, to yourself ) and just do what needs

to be done by signing up at \[URL\] right now so we can quit

screwing around and get down to business.”

You don’t have to be that direct, but you can. As long as you

care, you can get away with it. Remember, we don’t just

handle objections, we destroy them. I’ll revisit the money

objection again in a bit. Now, I transition to time:

“Now, for those of you who haven’t signed up yet and who,

from a financial point of view, feel comfortable knowing

you can make this investment without breaking a sweat,

your question is the real question because it ain’t about the

money—it’s about the time. See, money can be replenished,

but a minute gone is gone forever. You want to know what,

in addition to the monetary investment, is required of your

time. Here’s what I know about you: The first thing I know

is that you can make time for things that are worthwhile. In fact, you are here right now, right here, one hour and twenty-three minutes into this webinar, so I know you have some time. Do you have enough time? Well, time is the only thing that is given out equally to each and everyone in the world.

Did you know there is nothing else so evenly and fairly distributed as time? It’s not how much time you have, it’s what you do with the time that you have that matters. So here’s what I want you to do. If I can show you how to do this and save time (actually have more free time than you currently do) would you sign up then? Here’s what I want you to do.

Mentally, I want you to begin making a list of the five things you do consistently to try to get \[a certain, specific result\].

Next, I want you to order them from the most effective to the least effective thing you nd yourself doing often to move forward with \[solution\], with the least effective thing you currently do being number ve on your list. Do you see it?

Now, I want you to take a big red marker and cross that out. And in its place put \[product name\]. Because what you’re doing right now ain’t cutting it. If you knew for certain you could get \[some benet\], would you wake up fifteen minutes earlier ve days a week and go to bed fifteen minutes later?

Congratulations\! That’s all you need to get started, and get started you will. Go to \[URL\] right now because it’s time, and the less time you currently have in your life, the more time this will make for you.”

After I take a stab at both time and money, then I switch

to product-specific objections. These are the same objections we first brought up in the introduction section plus additional ones that have come up that you consider, if answered, could lead to a purchase. Here is how you can transition:

“Now that we’ve covered the investment and time commitment, and showed that anyone who is serious about \[benefit\] can make a go, what really matters are the following questions...”

In the Amazon webinar, the first question is “Can I do this from \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_?” For these, I like to use specific names of people who asked them. Even if the following transcripts aren’t perfectly situated for your product, pay attention to the structure of how I handle them:

“Lisa asks, ‘Is it truly possible to do this from anywhere in the world?’ Here’s the good news: yes, if you have an Internet connection. And it doesn’t have to be a very good one, as you saw in Basavaraj’s case. That’s actually one of the best selling points, because that means you can do this on the beach, you can do this while traveling, and you can do this part time from anywhere you want. Isn’t that wonderful?

That’s why, no matter where you are, you’re going to go to

\[URL\] and get started ASAP.”

Next objection:

“Todd asks, ‘Why would manufacturers sell to us instead of selling on Amazon directly?’ Great question, Todd\! The short answer is they just do. In every single case that you see a successful person making big money on Amazon, it’s because the manufacturer would rather supply them than sell to the end customer. It’s just the way the world works. If I had to guess, it’s because they are more focused on the manufacturing side—the factors of production, the raw materials, and the packaging—than on selling. Basically, their attitude is, ‘I’ll deal with you, you can deal with the thousands of customers you get as a result.’ It’s such a wonderful way this thing is set up, isn’t it? And you can start by going to \[URL\] right now.”

Next question:

“Barry is wondering about how technical you have to be to make this work because, as he puts it, he’s all thumbs when it comes to this Internet stuff. Well Barry, I got good news for you then. Do you have a smartphone? Do you know how to work it reasonably well to get what you want out of it? I bet you didn’t even have to read an instruction manual to make that happen either, right? Well, that’s Amazon. That’s why, unlike other things you may have had to try online, this is the opposite of that. And I think that’s one of the reasons so many more people are succeeding here who have never succeeded at anything in business before in their lives. Your success starts at \[URL\], where you can go and sign up right now.”

Now, I switch back to a money close, without actually answering anyone’s question.

“You know, this has helped so many people from all walks of life, especially those who nd themselves in a real tough financial situation. I’ve read about it, too—those people who wrote to us at support@rapidcrush.com telling me falsely that they would do it if only they had the money, but for some reason or other they’re currently going through a financial hardship. We don’t give up on them. The reality is there is no other way to change that financial situation than to buck up and find a way to make it happen. I know it’s uncomfortable if you have to ask someone to put up the money for you. But would you rather suffer that discomfort or have your already-bad financial situation get worse? I’m the last guy who likes to pay interest on a credit card, but when I started, that’s what I did. I got a rate increase on my credit card and all of a sudden that little extra wiggle room of capital made all the difference. I’ve found that people either have resources or they have to be resourceful. I’ve also found that it doesn’t take money to make money either. If it did, I’d still be painting houses for $12 an hour. If you have the resources, I’m sure you will sign up at \[URL\] right now. But if resources are tight, it’s time for you to be resourceful. I’m not asking you to buy a franchise here. A Dunkin’ Donuts franchise costs several-hundred-thousand dollars if you can meet their very high requirements. That is beyond most people’s grasp. But $4,997? Nah. You can do it if you want to. The truth is, the more resourceful you have to be to get signed up, the more resourceful you’ll be to make \[product\] work for you. Then I switch back to a product-specific question: “Tina was asking about competition. This uses a partial agreement frame—I agree there is competition, but I change the definition of what competition is in a way that supports the purchase of my product. Now, we go back to a time objection:

to start a business from scratch on Amazon.com. The best

I incorporated a powerful technique I learned from Ciald-

ini in his book, Pre-Suasion, into this close. When I was at

a mastermind where Cialdini came and gave a lecture, he

explained to us that if you wanted to make saying “yes” to

your offer seem like an easy and significant gesture, first

state something that is so much bigger in size and scope. The

example he gave was that we are ninety-three million miles

from the sun. Simply stating that major thing before asking

for whatever you’re going to ask can help get compliance. I

adapted that technique and used seven billion people, and

that 6.9 billion people will be missed, and then asked them

to make an investment. Relative comparison. You can make

almost anything seem like not a big deal when you compare

it to the distance from the sun or the size of the population.

related to the product or opportunity at hand before cycling

Here’s an exercise I recommend to you that did wonders for

me when I first started to do webinars. I call it “Dead Sleep”

theory. The theory is you can only truly be considered good

at webinars if someone could break into your house at night,

wake you up from a dead sleep, and ask you to rattle off

ve money objection closes and ve time objection closes

successfully. How, then, do you suppose you could make

that happen? Simple: rote memorization. I urge you to take

When I started, I didn’t have anything with webinars to

work off. What I did was get the book Secrets of Closing the

incompetent—if you always have to rely on reference material, you are consciously incompetent.
